Every node has exactly three neighbors." width="100%"} The generalized Petersen graph GP(n, k) (Coxeter, 1950; named by Watkins, 1969) has an outer cycle `u_0, ..., u_{n-1}`, an inner "star polygon" in which each `v_i` is joined to `v_{(i + k) mod n}`, and a spoke from every `u_i` to `v_i`. The Petersen graph is GP(5, 2), and the family takes in many of the famous cubic graphs: the prism GP(n, 1), the cube GP(4, 1), the dodecahedron GP(10, 2), the Desargues graph GP(10, 3), the Möbius-Kantor graph GP(8, 3) and the Nauru graph GP(12, 5). With `k < n / 2` the graph is cubic, with `2n` nodes and `3n` edges. With `k = n / 2` (for even `n`) each inner node's two chords coincide, so the inner nodes have degree 2 and there are `n / 2` fewer edges. GP(n, k) and GP(n, n - k) are the same graph, which is why `k` is limited to `n / 2`. Nodes are created in the order `u_0, ..., u_{n-1}, v_0, ..., v_{n-1}`, matching the node numbering of NetworkX's `generalized_petersen_graph()` (its node `i` is the `i`-th node created here). In a directed graph every edge points from the earlier-created node to the later one. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Generalized Petersen graphs are useful for: - a parametrized supply of cubic graphs, symmetric or not (GP(n, k) is vertex-transitive exactly when `k^2 = ±1 mod n` or `(n, k) = (10, 2)`; Frucht, Graver and Watkins, 1971) - test cases for coloring, Hamiltonicity and matching algorithms (GP(n, 2) is non-Hamiltonian exactly when `n = 5 mod 6`; Alspach, 1983) - examples and counterexamples in algebraic and topological graph theory ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes on each of the two rings. Must be at least `3`. [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Step of the inner star polygon. Must satisfy `1 <= k <= n / 2`. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` is less than `3`, or `k=` is not between `1` and `n / 2`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} GP(5, 2) is the Petersen graph: ::: {#6f262c09 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec gp = ec.Graph().add_generalized_petersen_graph(5, 2) gp.count_nodes(), gp.count_edges(), gp.is_isomorphic( ec.Graph().add_named_graph("petersen") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (10, 15, True) ``` ::: ::: Varying `k` with `n = 10` gives graphs of different girth: the prism GP(10, 1) has squares, the dodecahedron GP(10, 2) has pentagons, and the Desargues graph GP(10, 3) is bipartite with girth 6: ::: {#ae0c7b7a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} {k: ec.Graph().add_generalized_petersen_graph(10, k).girth() for k in (1, 2, 3)} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {1: 4, 2: 5, 3: 6} ``` ::: :::
